study.title: Psalm 75 God humbles the proud and exalts the righteous
study.overview: This psalm is a song of No?? no: gratitude and trust. The community begins to praise why God is near and because his admirable works are known; then the Lord himself speaks, stating that he will judge at the right time and that stability does not come from human force, but from him. The center of the psalm is the opposition between the pride of the wicked and the exaltation granted by God to the righteous. The tone is of worship, warning and hope: God sees arrogance, overthrows those who exalt and sustain his people.

outline.title: Praise for the presence of God and for his righteousness
outline.explanation: The first verses present the voice of the community grateful and then the divine answer. God is celebrated because his name is near and because he judges with righteousness at the appointed time. The image of the shaken land and the established pillars shows that even when everything seems unstable, the support of the world and its people depends on the Lord.

outline.title: Warning to the proud and announcement of judgment
outline.explanation: God speaks directly to the arrogant and the wicked, forbidding the exaltation of one's own power. The psalm teaches that human elevation comes from no direction of creation, but only from God, who slaughters one and raises another. The cup in the hand of the Lord symbolizes the inevitable judgment on the wicked, who will drink to the end the consequence of his rebellion.

outline.title: Right answer and final reversal
outline.explanation: After the proclamation of judgment, the psalmist assumes a permanent posture of praise to the God of Jacob. The outcome summarizes the moral reversal of the psalm: God cuts off the arrogance of the wicked and raises the righteous, whose face will be exalted.

study.context: The title identifies the psalm as being from Assafe, to the regent, with the musical indication "altachete." The notes provided observe that some interpreters relate the psalm to the moment David came to the throne after Saul's death, but this should be read as an interpretative hypothesis, not as an indisputable data of the text. The psalm itself, however, speaks of a situation in which the arrogance of the mighty is confronted by the righteousness of God.
study.theology: The psalm affirms God's sovereignty over history, about human authority, and moral judgment. exaltation is not a product of human merit, strength or location; it comes exclusively from the Lord, who rules as Judge. This confronts the self-reliance of the wicked and comforts the righteous, because the last word does not belong to human power, but to God. Also appears a theology of just retribution: pride is slaughtered, evil is treated with seriousness and divine justice does not fail, even though it is manifested in the appointed time of God. For a Protestant evangelical reading, the psalm calls God's people to praise, trust and wait with humility, without claiming for themselves the honor that belongs to the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm brings together community gratitude and the divine response, ensuring that God will act with righteousness in his time and that the Lord alone is the Judge who can exalt and humiliate.
The psalmist recognizes that the very elevation comes from God; therefore, whoever receives power must use it for good and not to exalt himself against the Lord.
The cup in the hand of the Lord represents the judgment against the wicked, a safe punishment for arrogance and oppression.

questions: In which areas of life have I trusted more in my own power than in the sovereign action of God?
How does the fact that God being the Judge changes the way I respond to injustice or arrogance around me?
Does my practice of praise reflect continuous gratitude, as in psalm, or just occasional recognition for the blessings received?
study.practice: During the week, identify a situation in which you feel tempted to promote, control results or fear influential people. Pray with sincerity, giving this area to the judgment and exaltation of God. Then practice a concrete action of humility: give credit to God for something you have received, refuse an arrogant attitude and manifest encouragement to a righteous or oppressed person, remembering that the Lord sustains yours.
study.uncertainty: The text does not inform with absolute historical certainty the context of composition; the connection with David's ascension after Saul appears only as a reading of commentators. Nor can it be possible to safely affirm, from this chapter alone, the exact identity of the wicked or the righteous in specific historical terms. The images of the cup and columns are symbolic and should be understood as the psalm itself presents them.
